note: Written to be spoken: one idea per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said, never as digits. Tool and flag names are spoken as their job, not their symbol. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step. Opens on the chapter bridge line and closes on the handoff line.

lines: Every clause so far answered what a query means.
Now: what actually happens between typing that query and getting an answer back.
Five separate stages carry your words to an actual answer, and each one is only allowed to know a little more than the one before it.
First, nothing but grammar. Does this even look like a valid sentence. No idea yet what any of the names refer to.
Then, meaning. Now it looks up every name you used, and learns exactly what table, what function, what operator you meant.
Then, rewriting. Anything built on a shortcut, like a view, gets quietly unfolded back into the real tables underneath it.
Then, choosing. Many different ways could compute the same answer, and one gets picked.
And only then... running it, for real, and handing back rows.
Here's the idea worth holding onto through everything in this part of the chapter.
What a query computes, and how it's actually carried out, are two separate layers.
The first layer is just the shape: filter, then join, then total. Nothing about which exact method does the filtering, or which exact method does the joining.
So, predict: for one single logical shape like that, is there usually only one physical way to carry it out?
answer: Scan every row, or hop straight to the ones that matter through an index... two different ways to do the exact same filter.
Loop through one side for every row of the other, or sort both sides first, or build a quick lookup table... three different ways to do the exact same join.
Same shape, same answer at the end. Genuinely different amounts of work to get there.

lines: And here's a detail that pays for itself constantly.
A way of reading a table doesn't just hand back rows. Sometimes it hands them back already sitting in a useful order... for free, as a side effect of how it reads them.
So if something later in the plan needed exactly that order anyway... what happens to the separate step that would normally have had to produce it?
answer: It simply disappears. There's nothing left for it to do.
One part of the plan already handed over the order the next part needed. Paying twice for the same thing would just be waste.
That's the entire trick behind a surprising number of fast plans: something upstream already did the work something downstream was about to ask for.

lines: So: five stages, each one knowing a little more than the last.
What a query means, and how it's actually run, are genuinely two different layers, and there's real choice in the second one.
And a useful order, earned once, doesn't need to be earned twice.
Right now, every plan has only ever meant exactly what it said.
Next: the rewrites that quietly turn one legal plan into a cheaper, equally legal one.
